newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's Santer says Renault in the wrong over closure.
newsitem.headline: EU's Santer says Renault in the wrong over closure.

text.p: European Commission president Jacques Santer said on Wednesday that Renault had handled the closure of its Belgian plant poorly and implicitly encouraged court action against the French car maker.
"Regardless of whether they did or did not follow directives, the spirit of the law was not respected," Santer said in a statement read to reporters by his spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas.
Asked if this could be interpreted as support for legal action against Renault, Van der Pas replied: "You can take that as encouragement,"
Earlier, the Commission reiterated Renault's decision to close the Volvoorde assembly plant was not a matter for its scrutiny but said it was clear "questions need to be answered".
"It seems the workers have been left with a fait accompli," said Barbara Nolan, spokeswoman for European social affairs commissioner Padraig Flynn.
"There are serious questions that need to be answered by Renault, but it is up to national authorities to pursue them."
Van der Pas added later: "Without prejudice to anything the Belgian authorities may undertake, it is up to the workers or any other interested party to take the issue to national courts."
Santer discussed the issue with Belgium's King Albert II during a meeting earlier on Wednesday and Van der Pas said both men expressed concern for the fate of the workers who will lose their jobs.
The decision to close the plant has been met by outrage from Belgian authorities, the Flanders regional government and trade unions.

It has sparked calls for a Belgian boycott of Renault cars and prompted the government to cancel an order for 150 Renault vehicles. Other officials have threatened to bar the company from public procurement tenders.
The European Commissioners are due to discuss the issue during their regular weekly meeting later on Wednesday, but Nolan stressed there appeared little the commission could do.

Flynn said two European directives which outlined how workers should be consulted in the event of a factory closure had been made law in Belgium and France and so it was up to national governments or trade unions to pursue the matter in national courts.
Willy Helin, spokesman for European Competition commissioner Karel van Miert, said it looked as if Renault may have a case to answer.

"His (Van Miert's) analysis of the explanations from several sources has led him to believe that Renault may not have followed the correct procedure," Helin said. "Speaking as an individual, a Belgian and a commissioner, he has formed his opinion."
Renault says the decision to close Vilvoorde -- with the loss of 3,100 direct jobs, was necessary to reduce costs and respond to competition.
